title: "NeuPL: Neural Population Learning"

en.text: In strategy games like StarCraft or poker, training a single "best" policy is meaningless: rock always loses to paper, and any lone strategy can be countered. To hold its ground in games like these, an agent needs a whole population of policies that keep each other in check. The catch is how that population is usually grown — one policy at a time. You freeze the existing policies, train a fresh policy from scratch to beat a mixture over them, and repeat.

This recipe is clean in a normal-form game like rock-paper-scissors, where a best response can be solved exactly. But real games are temporal and partially observed, so a best response can only be approximated with expensive deep reinforcement learning. That breaks the loop in two ways. Under a finite budget you can't tell a genuinely converged best response from one stuck on a local plateau, so iterations get truncated on a hand-crafted schedule and the population fills up with under-trained "good responses." And every new policy relearns basic skills — perception, memory, motor control — from scratch, which becomes intractable as opponents grow stronger.

The insight behind NeuPL (Neural Population Learning) is that these policies overlap enormously. They share perception, memory, and motor skills, so training them independently is wasteful. If a single model could hold the entire population and condition its behavior on which opponents it faces, the early skills it learns against weak opponents would directly bootstrap the discovery of exploiters to much stronger ones. This ICLR 2022 paper, from University College London and DeepMind, turns that idea into a unifying framework that keeps its convergence guarantees.

en.caption: Figure 1. Popular population-learning algorithms written as directed interaction graphs (bottom) or, equivalently, as meta-game mixture-strategy matrices Σ (top). A directed edge from policy i to j with weight σij means policy i optimizes against j with probability σij. Self-play, a strategic cycle, fictitious play, and PSRO-Nash are all just different choices of Σ within one framework.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07415　Project page: https://neupl.github.io/demo/
Where the old framework gets stuck

Why insist on a population at all? The reason is game-theoretic. In a purely cyclic game like rock-paper-scissors, getting "better" is relative: improving against one opponent means losing to another, so a single point strategy has nowhere to stand. The classic answer, Policy Space Response Oracles (PSRO), grows a population by repeatedly best-responding to a mixture over the existing strategies — but it trains them one at a time and discards the knowledge they could share. Empirical successes like the StarCraft league leaned on close to a thousand agents at enormous cost, which is exactly the case for a far more sample- and skill-efficient alternative.

NeuPL hands two normally hand-tuned knobs — the population size and the per-iteration training budget — back to the algorithm. Instead of a hand-crafted truncation schedule deciding when a policy counts as "done," a meta-graph solver decides the effective population size during training, while every policy shares the same underlying skills.
The method: one network, one interaction graph

Concretely, NeuPL trains a single opponent-conditioned network Πθ(·|o, σi). Each policy index i is paired with a meta-strategy vector σi — a probability distribution that says which other policies it should play against, and how often. The network maximizes a discounted return under a double expectation: first over the sampled opponent σj, then over the game dynamics induced by both policies, written J(σi) = E_{σj∼P(σi)} E_{a∼Πθ(·|o,σi), a'∼Πθ(·|o',σj)} [ Σ_t γ^t r_t ].

To optimize this by reinforcement learning, NeuPL jointly trains an opponent-conditioned action-value function Qθ, and additionally learns a payoff estimator φω that predicts the expected outcome of any policy pairing directly from the value function — so the full payoff matrix can be evaluated cheaply without replaying every matchup. The interaction graph Σ that assigns opponents can be a fixed matrix, which reproduces fictitious play, or adaptive, recomputed from the learned payoffs U by a meta-graph solver as Σ ← F(U), which reproduces PSRO-Nash. Because the graph, not a hand-crafted schedule, controls which objectives are active, the number of genuinely distinct policies grows on its own as the game demands. When two rows σi = σj coincide, their policies collapse into one, so the effective population size emerges automatically.

The paper backs this with a guarantee: for grounded, lower-triangular interaction graphs and a suitable meta-graph solver, NeuPL provably converges to an N-step best response, and with large enough N to a normal-form Nash equilibrium. In other words, it buys the efficiency of sharing and transfer without giving up the game-theoretic convergence that made the iterative methods trustworthy.
Watching it work in rock-paper-scissors

The clearest way to see NeuPL's dynamics is to put it back in rock-paper-scissors, where the whole population can be drawn directly on the strategy simplex. The figure below uses an adaptive interaction graph implementing PSRO-Nash, with an epoch every 10 iterations. Read the three rows separately: the top shows where each strategy sits in the R/P/S triangle, the middle is the learned payoff matrix between strategies, and the bottom is the interaction graph the solver produces as its response to that payoff matrix each epoch.

en.caption: Figure 3. NeuPL in rock-paper-scissors under an adaptive interaction graph implementing PSRO-Nash. (Top) the strategy space explored by the neural population over time; (middle) the learned payoff estimates between strategies; (bottom) the interaction-graph adjacency matrices produced as responses to the payoff matrix. New strategies are pushed toward the corners of the simplex as the payoff matrix and graph expand.

en.text: As training proceeds, new strategies are pushed one by one toward the corners of the simplex, a cyclic structure sharpens in the payoff matrix, and the interaction graph expands to match. This is what "let the solver decide who to train against" looks like in the simplest possible game. The real test is whether the same mechanism scales to harder domains.
Scaling to a spatiotemporal, partially observed game

Running-with-scissors lifts rock-paper-scissors into a spatiotemporal, partially observed setting. Players move around a grid world, collect rock, paper, and scissors resources, and see the world only through a narrow 4×4 first-person view, from which they must infer the opponent's hidden inventory. There is no exact best response to solve for here, exactly the regime where PSRO's hand-crafted truncation schedule is most fragile.

en.caption: Figure 4. A NeuPL population developing an increasingly sophisticated, diverse set of policies in running-with-scissors. The interaction graph is refreshed every 1,000 gradient updates (an epoch). (Top) the learned payoff estimates U between policies as training progresses; (bottom) the interaction graph Σ ← FPSRO-N(U) produced in response to the payoff matrix.

en.text: The payoff matrix U grows structure out of a blank start and the interaction graph Σ expands alongside it, evidence that the population keeps discovering new mutually-countering strategies — all inside a single network, where the perception and control skills learned early are reused again and again by later policies.
The headline result: more efficient and more robust

The most telling comparison pits a NeuPL population directly against PSRO baselines representing the same set of policies. The figure below only makes sense if you read both axes together: the solid curves are Relative Population Performance (higher means better able to exploit the opponent), and the dashed purple line is the effective population size on the right axis.

en.caption: Figure 7. Relative Population Performance between a NeuPL population and the policy populations obtained by PSRO baselines; each PSRO variant is repeated over 3 trials (shaded). The dashed purple line is the effective population size: the rise in relative performance coincides with effective size growing from 5 to 8.

en.text: Two things stand out. First, a NeuPL population capped at 8 policies exploits PSRO populations of the same 8 policies — even when each PSRO iteration was given 2× the gradient updates. Second, and more importantly, the gain in relative performance coincides with the effective population size climbing from 5 to 8. That timing suggests the improvement comes from genuinely discovering new strategies rather than overfitting to old ones. Both the continued-training and from-scratch PSRO variants prove equally exploitable, which suggests they fail to build reusable representations.
Why it gets cheaper: the role of transfer

NeuPL's most counterintuitive property is that discovering new strategies gets easier, not harder, as the population expands. A dedicated ablation isolates transfer to test this. A fresh agent is initialized either from scratch or by transferring the encoder and memory components of a NeuPL network trained to epoch 1,000, then asked to beat fixed Nash mixtures of increasing strength.

en.caption: Figure 6. Transferring from a NeuPL agent (left: only the green Encoder and Memory are carried over) into a fresh agent that must learn to exploit fixed Nash mixtures. Red is trained from random initialization; green transfers from epoch 1,000. Against an easily exploitable n=2 mixture the random-init agent catches up; against strong n=4 and n=7 mixtures it barely learns even with prolonged training, while transfer readily finds the exploit. Each experiment is repeated five times.

en.text: Against an easily exploitable two-policy mixture, even the from-scratch agent eventually finds a counter, just more slowly. But against competent mixtures over four or seven policies, the randomly initialized agent barely learns at all despite prolonged training, while the agent that transferred the encoder and memory readily discovers the exploit. This is the paper's central claim made concrete: the larger the population, the thicker the shared skill base, and the easier it becomes to find the next new strategy.
All the way up to MuJoCo Football

Finally, to show the framework survives real scale, the paper applies NeuPL to 2v2 MuJoCo Football — a Game-of-Skills that demands continuous motor control and team coordination at once, with latent strategic cycles underneath.

en.caption: Figure 8. NeuPL implementing FPSRO-N in 2v2 MuJoCo Football. Left: the learned payoff matrices and interaction graphs at successive training epochs. Right: red/blue/white traces are the red players, blue players, and the ball, illustrating the counter relationships that emerge between policies.

en.text: Even in this regime, where continuous control and team play are entangled, the payoff matrix grows a clear cyclic structure and the trajectory traces show genuine counter relationships between policies. The same "one network holds the whole population" recipe carries all the way from rock-paper-scissors up to football.

en.text: Takeaway and honest boundaries

The one-line takeaway: hold the whole population inside a single opponent-conditioned network, let the interaction graph decide who trains against whom, and skills transfer for free across policies. That turns population learning from a sequence of wasteful from-scratch iterations into one transfer-rich training run — cheaper, still convergent, and with the surprising bonus that novel strategies become more accessible, not less, as the neural population grows.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly. The convergence guarantee applies to grounded, lower-triangular interaction graphs with a suitable solver; raising the maximum population cap beyond 8 buys only marginal improvement in exploitability; and the MuJoCo Football result is more a qualitative demonstration of feasibility than a systematic benchmark win. Even so, the through-line — carry an entire population in one conditional model — points a clear and economical way toward pushing game-theoretic population learning into genuinely complex games.

zh.text: 在 StarCraft、扑克这类策略博弈里，只训练一个「最强策略」是没有意义的：石头总会输给布，任何单一策略都能被针对。要在这类博弈里稳住阵脚，模型需要的是一整支互相制衡的策略群（population）。问题在于，主流做法是把这支群「一个一个」养大——每次固定住已有的策略，再从头训练一个新策略去打败它们的混合，如此循环。

这套流程在石头剪刀布这样的标准式（normal-form）小游戏里很干净，因为最优反应（best response）可以精确求解。但真实博弈是时序的、部分可观测的，最优反应只能用昂贵的深度强化学习去近似。于是两个麻烦同时出现：算力有限时，你分不清一个策略是真的收敛了，还是卡在局部平台，只能凭手工设定的时间表提前截断训练，把一批「训练不足」的弱策略塞进群里；更糟的是，每个新策略都要从零重新学会走路、看图、操控这些基本功，对手越强，这件事越算不动。

NeuPL（Neural Population Learning）给出的思路很直接：这些策略之间的重叠其实极大——它们共享感知、记忆和运动技能，分开训练本身就是浪费。如果一个网络能同时装下整支策略群，并根据「该打谁」来切换自己的行为，那么对弱对手学到的早期技能，就能直接为发现针对强对手的克制策略打好底子。这篇发表于 ICLR 2022、来自伦敦大学学院（UCL）与 DeepMind 的工作，把这个想法做成了一个带收敛保证的统一框架。

zh.caption: 图1 常见的种群学习算法都可以写成同一种「交互图」（下方有向图）或等价的元博弈混合策略矩阵 Σ（上方矩阵）。图中从策略 i 指向 j、权重为 σij 的有向边，表示策略 i 以概率 σij 去对抗 j。自博弈、策略循环、虚拟博弈、PSRO-Nash 只是同一框架下 Σ 的不同取值。

zh.text: 论文链接：https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07415　项目主页：https://neupl.github.io/demo/
老框架卡在哪里

为什么非要一支策略群？根源在博弈论：像石头剪刀布这样纯循环（cyclic）的博弈里，「变强」是相对的——你对某个对手变强，就意味着对另一个对手变弱，单点策略无处安放。经典的 PSRO（Policy Space Response Oracles）正是用「群」来处理这种循环：反复训练新策略去最优反应已有策略的混合。但它把策略一个一个训练，并丢弃了它们之间本可共享的知识。像 StarCraft 联赛那样的成功案例，动用了接近一千个智能体、代价惊人，这恰恰说明：我们需要一个在样本和技能上都高效得多的替代方案。
NeuPL 把两个原本手工设定的旋钮——种群规模、每轮训练预算——交还给算法本身。它不再靠人为的截断时间表决定「练到什么程度算一个新策略」，而是让元博弈求解器（meta-graph solver）在训练中决定有效的种群规模，同时让所有策略共享底层技能。
方法：一个网络，一张交互图

具体来说，NeuPL 只训练一个「对手条件化」的网络 Πθ(·|o, σi)。每个策略序号 i 都配一个元策略向量 σi，它是一个概率分布，规定这个策略应该以多大比例去对抗其他哪些策略。网络要最大化的是一个双重期望下的折扣回报：先对采样到的对手 σj 取期望，再对由双方策略共同决定的博弈动态取期望，即 J(σi) = E_{σj∼P(σi)} E_{a∼Πθ(·|o,σi), a'∼Πθ(·|o',σj)} [ Σ_t γ^t r_t ]。

为了用强化学习优化它，NeuPL 联合训练一个对手条件化的动作价值函数 Qθ；此外还额外学一个收益估计器（payoff estimator）φω，直接从价值函数预测任意一对策略交手的期望结果，这样整张收益矩阵就能廉价地估出来，而不必把每一组对局都重放一遍。分配对手的这张交互图 Σ，既可以是一个固定矩阵（复现虚拟博弈 fictitious play），也可以是自适应的——由元图求解器根据学到的收益 U 重新计算 Σ ← F(U)（复现 PSRO-Nash）。关键在于：决定「哪些目标此刻生效」的是这张图，而不是手工时间表，所以真正互不相同的策略数量会随博弈需要自行增长。当两行 σi = σj 完全相同，对应的策略就会坍缩成同一个，于是「有效种群规模」自然浮现出来。
论文进一步证明：对于「接地的」下三角交互图与合适的元图求解器，NeuPL 会收敛到 N 步最优反应；当 N 足够大时，收敛到标准式的纳什均衡。换句话说，它在获得共享与迁移带来的效率的同时，并没有丢掉博弈论上的收敛保证。
在石头剪刀布里看清它怎么工作
要理解 NeuPL 的动态，最直观的办法是把它放回石头剪刀布，因为整支策略群可以直接画在策略单纯形（simplex）上。下图用一个实现 PSRO-Nash 的自适应交互图来训练，每 10 次迭代算一个 epoch。看图时请把三行分开读：最上面一行是策略在 R/P/S 三角形里的位置，中间是网络学到的策略间收益矩阵，最下面是作为收益矩阵响应而生成的交互图（邻接矩阵）。

zh.caption: 图3 采用实现 PSRO-Nash 的自适应交互图后，NeuPL 在石头剪刀布中的演化。（上）随时间被神经种群探索到的策略空间；（中）种群策略之间学到的收益估计；（下）作为对收益矩阵的响应而生成的交互图邻接矩阵。可见新策略被逐步推向三角形边角，收益矩阵和交互图随之扩展。

zh.text: 随着训练推进，新策略被一个个推向单纯形的边角，收益矩阵里出现越来越清晰的循环结构，交互图也随之扩展——这正是「让求解器决定该练谁」在最简单博弈里的可视化。同一套机制放大到更难的域，才是这篇论文真正要证明的事。
放大到时空、部分可观测的博弈
running-with-scissors 把石头剪刀布抬进了一个时空、部分可观测的设定：玩家在格子世界里移动，采集石头、布、剪刀三种资源，而且只能通过一个 4×4 的第一人称狭窄视野观察世界，必须从中推断对手隐藏的库存。这里没有精确最优反应可解，正是 PSRO 手工截断最脆弱的地方。

zh.caption: 图4 在 running-with-scissors 中，一支 NeuPL 种群逐步发展出越来越复杂、越来越多样的策略集合。交互图每 1,000 次梯度更新（一个 epoch）刷新一次。（上）随训练推进，神经种群策略之间学到的收益估计 U；（下）作为对收益矩阵响应而生成的交互图 Σ ← FPSRO-N(U)。

zh.text: 收益矩阵 U 从一片空白逐渐长出结构，交互图 Σ 也随之扩展，说明种群确实在持续发现能互相克制的新策略——而这一切都发生在同一个网络内部，早期学到的感知与操控技能被后来的策略反复复用。
核心结果：更省，也更稳
最能说明问题的对照，是把 NeuPL 种群直接拿去打代表同样策略集合的 PSRO 基线。下图的关键在于两条轴要一起看：黑色实线群是相对种群表现（Relative Population Performance，越高表示越能压制对手），紫色虚线是有效种群规模（右轴）。

zh.caption: 图7 一支 NeuPL 种群与 PSRO 基线得到的策略种群之间的相对种群表现。每个 PSRO 变体重复 3 次试验，以阴影表示。紫色虚线为有效种群规模：相对表现的上升与有效种群规模从 5 增长到 8 同步发生。

zh.text: 结论有两层。其一，一支最大规模为 8 的 NeuPL 种群，能够压制由同样 8 个策略构成的 PSRO 种群——即便这些 PSRO 基线每轮迭代拿到了 2 倍的梯度更新。其二，也是更重要的一点：相对表现的提升，与有效种群规模从 5 增长到 8 是同步发生的。这说明性能的改善来自真正发现了新策略，而不是在旧策略上过拟合。无论是持续训练还是从零重训的 PSRO 变体，都同样容易被压制，暗示它们没有建立起可复用的表征。
为什么会更省：迁移的作用
NeuPL 最反直觉的性质，是随着种群变大，发现新策略反而变得更容易，而不是更难。一个专门的消融实验把「迁移」单独拎出来验证：让一个新智能体分别以两种方式初始化——完全随机，或者从一个训练到第 1,000 epoch 的 NeuPL 网络迁移其编码器（encoder）与记忆（memory）组件——再要求它去打败强度递增的固定纳什混合策略。

zh.caption: 图6 从不同 epoch 的 NeuPL 智能体向新智能体迁移，再让其学习克制固定纳什混合（左侧为网络结构，仅迁移绿色的 Encoder 与 Memory）。红色为随机初始化从头训练，绿色为从第 1,000 epoch 迁移。面对 n=2 的易剥削混合，随机初始化也能追上；但面对 n=4、n=7 的强混合，随机初始化即便长时间训练也几乎学不动，迁移则能顺利找到克制策略。每个实验重复 5 次。

zh.text: 面对一个只有 2 个策略、容易被剥削的混合，即便是随机初始化的智能体最终也能找到克制手段，只是更慢。但一旦对手是覆盖 4 个乃至 7 个策略的强混合，随机初始化的智能体即使长时间训练也几乎学不动，而迁移了编码器与记忆的智能体却能顺利发现克制策略。这正是 NeuPL 的核心卖点在实验上的落点：种群越大，共享的技能底座越厚，发现新策略反而越轻松。
一路放大到 MuJoCo Football
最后，为了证明框架能扛住真正的规模，论文把 NeuPL 用在了 2v2 的 MuJoCo Football 上——一个「技能博弈」（Game-of-Skills），既要求连续的运动控制，又要求团队协作，还藏着隐性的策略循环。

zh.caption: 图8 NeuPL 以 FPSRO-N 在 2v2 MuJoCo Football 中的表现。左侧为不同训练 epoch 下学到的收益矩阵与交互图；右侧红/蓝/白轨迹分别对应红方、蓝方球员与球，展示了不同策略之间出现的克制关系。

zh.text: 在这个连续控制与团队协作交织的域里，收益矩阵同样长出了清晰的循环结构，右侧轨迹图也显示出策略之间真实的克制关系——同一套「一个网络装下整支种群」的配方，从石头剪刀布一路撑到了足球。
关键数字一览

zh.text: 小结与边界
NeuPL 的一句话总结是：把整支策略群装进一个对手条件化的网络，让交互图决定谁和谁对练，技能便在策略之间免费流动。这把种群学习从「一轮轮从零重来」的浪费流程，变成了一次「充满迁移」的联合训练，既降低了成本，又保留了收敛保证，还带来一个最反直觉的好处——随着神经种群扩张，发现新策略变得更容易，而不是更难。
需要保持清醒的边界也很明确：论文的收敛保证针对的是接地的下三角交互图与合适的求解器，把最大种群上限提升到 8 以上，对可剥削性的改善也只是边际的；MuJoCo Football 上的结果更多是定性的可行性展示，而非大规模基准上的系统性胜负。即便如此，「用一个条件模型承载整支种群」这条主线，为把博弈论式的种群学习真正推向复杂真实博弈，给出了一个清晰而经济的方向。

en.title: ICLR 2022 | NeuPL: Fitting a Whole Population of Policies Into One Network
en.subtitle: UCL and DeepMind unify self-play, fictitious play, and PSRO in a single conditional network — with convergence guarantees and skills that transfer for free

zh.title: ICLR 2022 | 把一整支策略群装进一个网络：NeuPL 让种群学习不再从零重来
zh.subtitle: UCL 与 DeepMind 提出 Neural Population Learning，用一个条件网络统一自博弈、虚拟博弈与 PSRO，并给出收敛保证

en.text: In strategy games like StarCraft or poker, training a single "best" policy is meaningless: rock always loses to paper, and any lone strategy can be countered. To hold its ground in games like these, an agent needs a whole population of policies that keep each other in check. The catch is how that population is usually grown — one policy at a time. You freeze the existing policies, train a fresh policy from scratch to beat a mixture over them, and repeat.

This recipe is clean in a normal-form game like rock-paper-scissors, where a best response can be solved exactly. But real games are temporal and partially observed, so a best response can only be approximated with expensive deep reinforcement learning. That breaks the loop in two ways. Under a finite budget you can't tell a genuinely converged best response from one stuck on a local plateau, so iterations get truncated on a hand-crafted schedule and the population fills up with under-trained "good responses." And every new policy relearns basic skills — perception, memory, motor control — from scratch, which becomes intractable as opponents grow stronger.

The insight behind NeuPL (Neural Population Learning) is that these policies overlap enormously. They share perception, memory, and motor skills, so training them independently is wasteful. If a single model could hold the entire population and condition its behavior on which opponents it faces, the early skills it learns against weak opponents would directly bootstrap the discovery of exploiters to much stronger ones. This ICLR 2022 paper, from University College London and DeepMind, turns that idea into a unifying framework that keeps its convergence guarantees.

en.caption: Figure 1. Popular population-learning algorithms written as directed interaction graphs (bottom) or, equivalently, as meta-game mixture-strategy matrices Σ (top). A directed edge from policy i to j with weight σij means policy i optimizes against j with probability σij. Self-play, a strategic cycle, fictitious play, and PSRO-Nash are all just different choices of Σ within one framework.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07415　Project page: https://neupl.github.io/demo/

zh.text: 在 StarCraft、扑克这类策略博弈里，只训练一个「最强策略」是没有意义的：石头总会输给布，任何单一策略都能被针对。要在这类博弈里稳住阵脚，模型需要的是一整支互相制衡的策略群（population）。问题在于，主流做法是把这支群「一个一个」养大——每次固定住已有的策略，再从头训练一个新策略去打败它们的混合，如此循环。

这套流程在石头剪刀布这样的标准式（normal-form）小游戏里很干净，因为最优反应（best response）可以精确求解。但真实博弈是时序的、部分可观测的，最优反应只能用昂贵的深度强化学习去近似。于是两个麻烦同时出现：算力有限时，你分不清一个策略是真的收敛了，还是卡在局部平台，只能凭手工设定的时间表提前截断训练，把一批「训练不足」的弱策略塞进群里；更糟的是，每个新策略都要从零重新学会走路、看图、操控这些基本功，对手越强，这件事越算不动。

NeuPL（Neural Population Learning）给出的思路很直接：这些策略之间的重叠其实极大——它们共享感知、记忆和运动技能，分开训练本身就是浪费。如果一个网络能同时装下整支策略群，并根据「该打谁」来切换自己的行为，那么对弱对手学到的早期技能，就能直接为发现针对强对手的克制策略打好底子。这篇发表于 ICLR 2022、来自伦敦大学学院（UCL）与 DeepMind 的工作，把这个想法做成了一个带收敛保证的统一框架。

zh.caption: 图1 常见的种群学习算法都可以写成同一种「交互图」（下方有向图）或等价的元博弈混合策略矩阵 Σ（上方矩阵）。图中从策略 i 指向 j、权重为 σij 的有向边，表示策略 i 以概率 σij 去对抗 j。自博弈、策略循环、虚拟博弈、PSRO-Nash 只是同一框架下 Σ 的不同取值。

en.caption: Figure 1. Popular population-learning algorithms written as directed interaction graphs (bottom) or, equivalently, as meta-game mixture-strategy matrices Σ (top). A directed edge from policy i to j with weight σij means policy i optimizes against j with probability σij. Self-play, a strategic cycle, fictitious play, and PSRO-Nash are all just different choices of Σ within one framework.

en.text: Where the old framework gets stuck

Why insist on a population at all? The reason is game-theoretic. In a purely cyclic game like rock-paper-scissors, getting "better" is relative: improving against one opponent means losing to another, so a single point strategy has nowhere to stand. The classic answer, Policy Space Response Oracles (PSRO), grows a population by repeatedly best-responding to a mixture over the existing strategies — but it trains them one at a time and discards the knowledge they could share. Empirical successes like the StarCraft league leaned on close to a thousand agents at enormous cost, which is exactly the case for a far more sample- and skill-efficient alternative.

NeuPL hands two normally hand-tuned knobs — the population size and the per-iteration training budget — back to the algorithm. Instead of a hand-crafted truncation schedule deciding when a policy counts as "done," a meta-graph solver decides the effective population size during training, while every policy shares the same underlying skills.

zh.caption: 图1 常见的种群学习算法都可以写成同一种「交互图」（下方有向图）或等价的元博弈混合策略矩阵 Σ（上方矩阵）。图中从策略 i 指向 j、权重为 σij 的有向边，表示策略 i 以概率 σij 去对抗 j。自博弈、策略循环、虚拟博弈、PSRO-Nash 只是同一框架下 Σ 的不同取值。

zh.text: 老框架卡在哪里

为什么非要一支策略群？根源在博弈论：像石头剪刀布这样纯循环（cyclic）的博弈里，「变强」是相对的——你对某个对手变强，就意味着对另一个对手变弱，单点策略无处安放。经典的 PSRO（Policy Space Response Oracles）正是用「群」来处理这种循环：反复训练新策略去最优反应已有策略的混合。但它把策略一个一个训练，并丢弃了它们之间本可共享的知识。像 StarCraft 联赛那样的成功案例，动用了接近一千个智能体、代价惊人，这恰恰说明：我们需要一个在样本和技能上都高效得多的替代方案。
NeuPL 把两个原本手工设定的旋钮——种群规模、每轮训练预算——交还给算法本身。它不再靠人为的截断时间表决定「练到什么程度算一个新策略」，而是让元博弈求解器（meta-graph solver）在训练中决定有效的种群规模，同时让所有策略共享底层技能。

en.caption: Figure 3. NeuPL in rock-paper-scissors under an adaptive interaction graph implementing PSRO-Nash. (Top) the strategy space explored by the neural population over time; (middle) the learned payoff estimates between strategies; (bottom) the interaction-graph adjacency matrices produced as responses to the payoff matrix. New strategies are pushed toward the corners of the simplex as the payoff matrix and graph expand.

en.text: Where the old framework gets stuck

Why insist on a population at all? The reason is game-theoretic. In a purely cyclic game like rock-paper-scissors, getting "better" is relative: improving against one opponent means losing to another, so a single point strategy has nowhere to stand. The classic answer, Policy Space Response Oracles (PSRO), grows a population by repeatedly best-responding to a mixture over the existing strategies — but it trains them one at a time and discards the knowledge they could share. Empirical successes like the StarCraft league leaned on close to a thousand agents at enormous cost, which is exactly the case for a far more sample- and skill-efficient alternative.

NeuPL hands two normally hand-tuned knobs — the population size and the per-iteration training budget — back to the algorithm. Instead of a hand-crafted truncation schedule deciding when a policy counts as "done," a meta-graph solver decides the effective population size during training, while every policy shares the same underlying skills.
The method: one network, one interaction graph

Concretely, NeuPL trains a single opponent-conditioned network Πθ(·|o, σi). Each policy index i is paired with a meta-strategy vector σi — a probability distribution that says which other policies it should play against, and how often. The network maximizes a discounted return under a double expectation: first over the sampled opponent σj, then over the game dynamics induced by both policies, written J(σi) = E_{σj∼P(σi)} E_{a∼Πθ(·|o,σi), a'∼Πθ(·|o',σj)} [ Σ_t γ^t r_t ].

To optimize this by reinforcement learning, NeuPL jointly trains an opponent-conditioned action-value function Qθ, and additionally learns a payoff estimator φω that predicts the expected outcome of any policy pairing directly from the value function — so the full payoff matrix can be evaluated cheaply without replaying every matchup. The interaction graph Σ that assigns opponents can be a fixed matrix, which reproduces fictitious play, or adaptive, recomputed from the learned payoffs U by a meta-graph solver as Σ ← F(U), which reproduces PSRO-Nash. Because the graph, not a hand-crafted schedule, controls which objectives are active, the number of genuinely distinct policies grows on its own as the game demands. When two rows σi = σj coincide, their policies collapse into one, so the effective population size emerges automatically.

The paper backs this with a guarantee: for grounded, lower-triangular interaction graphs and a suitable meta-graph solver, NeuPL provably converges to an N-step best response, and with large enough N to a normal-form Nash equilibrium. In other words, it buys the efficiency of sharing and transfer without giving up the game-theoretic convergence that made the iterative methods trustworthy.

为什么非要一支策略群？根源在博弈论：像石头剪刀布这样纯循环（cyclic）的博弈里，「变强」是相对的——你对某个对手变强，就意味着对另一个对手变弱，单点策略无处安放。经典的 PSRO（Policy Space Response Oracles）正是用「群」来处理这种循环：反复训练新策略去最优反应已有策略的混合。但它把策略一个一个训练，并丢弃了它们之间本可共享的知识。像 StarCraft 联赛那样的成功案例，动用了接近一千个智能体、代价惊人，这恰恰说明：我们需要一个在样本和技能上都高效得多的替代方案。
NeuPL 把两个原本手工设定的旋钮——种群规模、每轮训练预算——交还给算法本身。它不再靠人为的截断时间表决定「练到什么程度算一个新策略」，而是让元博弈求解器（meta-graph solver）在训练中决定有效的种群规模，同时让所有策略共享底层技能。
方法：一个网络，一张交互图

具体来说，NeuPL 只训练一个「对手条件化」的网络 Πθ(·|o, σi)。每个策略序号 i 都配一个元策略向量 σi，它是一个概率分布，规定这个策略应该以多大比例去对抗其他哪些策略。网络要最大化的是一个双重期望下的折扣回报：先对采样到的对手 σj 取期望，再对由双方策略共同决定的博弈动态取期望，即 J(σi) = E_{σj∼P(σi)} E_{a∼Πθ(·|o,σi), a'∼Πθ(·|o',σj)} [ Σ_t γ^t r_t ]。

为了用强化学习优化它，NeuPL 联合训练一个对手条件化的动作价值函数 Qθ；此外还额外学一个收益估计器（payoff estimator）φω，直接从价值函数预测任意一对策略交手的期望结果，这样整张收益矩阵就能廉价地估出来，而不必把每一组对局都重放一遍。分配对手的这张交互图 Σ，既可以是一个固定矩阵（复现虚拟博弈 fictitious play），也可以是自适应的——由元图求解器根据学到的收益 U 重新计算 Σ ← F(U)（复现 PSRO-Nash）。关键在于：决定「哪些目标此刻生效」的是这张图，而不是手工时间表，所以真正互不相同的策略数量会随博弈需要自行增长。当两行 σi = σj 完全相同，对应的策略就会坍缩成同一个，于是「有效种群规模」自然浮现出来。
论文进一步证明：对于「接地的」下三角交互图与合适的元图求解器，NeuPL 会收敛到 N 步最优反应；当 N 足够大时，收敛到标准式的纳什均衡。换句话说，它在获得共享与迁移带来的效率的同时，并没有丢掉博弈论上的收敛保证。

zh.subtitle: UCL 与 DeepMind 提出 Neural Population Learning，用一个条件网络统一自博弈、虚拟博弈与 PSRO，并给出收敛保证

en.caption: Figure 1. Popular population-learning algorithms written as directed interaction graphs (bottom) or, equivalently, as meta-game mixture-strategy matrices Σ (top). A directed edge from policy i to j with weight σij means policy i optimizes against j with probability σij. Self-play, a strategic cycle, fictitious play, and PSRO-Nash are all just different choices of Σ within one framework.

en.text: Takeaway and honest boundaries

The one-line takeaway: hold the whole population inside a single opponent-conditioned network, let the interaction graph decide who trains against whom, and skills transfer for free across policies. That turns population learning from a sequence of wasteful from-scratch iterations into one transfer-rich training run — cheaper, still convergent, and with the surprising bonus that novel strategies become more accessible, not less, as the neural population grows.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly. The convergence guarantee applies to grounded, lower-triangular interaction graphs with a suitable solver; raising the maximum population cap beyond 8 buys only marginal improvement in exploitability; and the MuJoCo Football result is more a qualitative demonstration of feasibility than a systematic benchmark win. Even so, the through-line — carry an entire population in one conditional model — points a clear and economical way toward pushing game-theoretic population learning into genuinely complex games.

zh.caption: 图1 常见的种群学习算法都可以写成同一种「交互图」（下方有向图）或等价的元博弈混合策略矩阵 Σ（上方矩阵）。图中从策略 i 指向 j、权重为 σij 的有向边，表示策略 i 以概率 σij 去对抗 j。自博弈、策略循环、虚拟博弈、PSRO-Nash 只是同一框架下 Σ 的不同取值。

zh.text: 小结与边界
NeuPL 的一句话总结是：把整支策略群装进一个对手条件化的网络，让交互图决定谁和谁对练，技能便在策略之间免费流动。这把种群学习从「一轮轮从零重来」的浪费流程，变成了一次「充满迁移」的联合训练，既降低了成本，又保留了收敛保证，还带来一个最反直觉的好处——随着神经种群扩张，发现新策略变得更容易，而不是更难。
需要保持清醒的边界也很明确：论文的收敛保证针对的是接地的下三角交互图与合适的求解器，把最大种群上限提升到 8 以上，对可剥削性的改善也只是边际的；MuJoCo Football 上的结果更多是定性的可行性展示，而非大规模基准上的系统性胜负。即便如此，「用一个条件模型承载整支种群」这条主线，为把博弈论式的种群学习真正推向复杂真实博弈，给出了一个清晰而经济的方向。

en.text: Scaling to a spatiotemporal, partially observed game

Running-with-scissors lifts rock-paper-scissors into a spatiotemporal, partially observed setting. Players move around a grid world, collect rock, paper, and scissors resources, and see the world only through a narrow 4×4 first-person view, from which they must infer the opponent's hidden inventory. There is no exact best response to solve for here, exactly the regime where PSRO's hand-crafted truncation schedule is most fragile.

en.caption: Figure 4. A NeuPL population developing an increasingly sophisticated, diverse set of policies in running-with-scissors. The interaction graph is refreshed every 1,000 gradient updates (an epoch). (Top) the learned payoff estimates U between policies as training progresses; (bottom) the interaction graph Σ ← FPSRO-N(U) produced in response to the payoff matrix.

en.text: The payoff matrix U grows structure out of a blank start and the interaction graph Σ expands alongside it, evidence that the population keeps discovering new mutually-countering strategies — all inside a single network, where the perception and control skills learned early are reused again and again by later policies.
The headline result: more efficient and more robust

The most telling comparison pits a NeuPL population directly against PSRO baselines representing the same set of policies. The figure below only makes sense if you read both axes together: the solid curves are Relative Population Performance (higher means better able to exploit the opponent), and the dashed purple line is the effective population size on the right axis.

en.caption: Figure 7. Relative Population Performance between a NeuPL population and the policy populations obtained by PSRO baselines; each PSRO variant is repeated over 3 trials (shaded). The dashed purple line is the effective population size: the rise in relative performance coincides with effective size growing from 5 to 8.

en.text: Two things stand out. First, a NeuPL population capped at 8 policies exploits PSRO populations of the same 8 policies — even when each PSRO iteration was given 2× the gradient updates. Second, and more importantly, the gain in relative performance coincides with the effective population size climbing from 5 to 8. That timing suggests the improvement comes from genuinely discovering new strategies rather than overfitting to old ones. Both the continued-training and from-scratch PSRO variants prove equally exploitable, which suggests they fail to build reusable representations.

zh.text: 方法：一个网络，一张交互图

具体来说，NeuPL 只训练一个「对手条件化」的网络 Πθ(·|o, σi)。每个策略序号 i 都配一个元策略向量 σi，它是一个概率分布，规定这个策略应该以多大比例去对抗其他哪些策略。网络要最大化的是一个双重期望下的折扣回报：先对采样到的对手 σj 取期望，再对由双方策略共同决定的博弈动态取期望，即 J(σi) = E_{σj∼P(σi)} E_{a∼Πθ(·|o,σi), a'∼Πθ(·|o',σj)} [ Σ_t γ^t r_t ]。

为了用强化学习优化它，NeuPL 联合训练一个对手条件化的动作价值函数 Qθ；此外还额外学一个收益估计器（payoff estimator）φω，直接从价值函数预测任意一对策略交手的期望结果，这样整张收益矩阵就能廉价地估出来，而不必把每一组对局都重放一遍。分配对手的这张交互图 Σ，既可以是一个固定矩阵（复现虚拟博弈 fictitious play），也可以是自适应的——由元图求解器根据学到的收益 U 重新计算 Σ ← F(U)（复现 PSRO-Nash）。关键在于：决定「哪些目标此刻生效」的是这张图，而不是手工时间表，所以真正互不相同的策略数量会随博弈需要自行增长。当两行 σi = σj 完全相同，对应的策略就会坍缩成同一个，于是「有效种群规模」自然浮现出来。
论文进一步证明：对于「接地的」下三角交互图与合适的元图求解器，NeuPL 会收敛到 N 步最优反应；当 N 足够大时，收敛到标准式的纳什均衡。换句话说，它在获得共享与迁移带来的效率的同时，并没有丢掉博弈论上的收敛保证。
在石头剪刀布里看清它怎么工作
要理解 NeuPL 的动态，最直观的办法是把它放回石头剪刀布，因为整支策略群可以直接画在策略单纯形（simplex）上。下图用一个实现 PSRO-Nash 的自适应交互图来训练，每 10 次迭代算一个 epoch。看图时请把三行分开读：最上面一行是策略在 R/P/S 三角形里的位置，中间是网络学到的策略间收益矩阵，最下面是作为收益矩阵响应而生成的交互图（邻接矩阵）。

zh.caption: 图3 采用实现 PSRO-Nash 的自适应交互图后，NeuPL 在石头剪刀布中的演化。（上）随时间被神经种群探索到的策略空间；（中）种群策略之间学到的收益估计；（下）作为对收益矩阵的响应而生成的交互图邻接矩阵。可见新策略被逐步推向三角形边角，收益矩阵和交互图随之扩展。

zh.text: 随着训练推进，新策略被一个个推向单纯形的边角，收益矩阵里出现越来越清晰的循环结构，交互图也随之扩展——这正是「让求解器决定该练谁」在最简单博弈里的可视化。同一套机制放大到更难的域，才是这篇论文真正要证明的事。

zh.title: ICLR 2022 | 把一整支策略群装进一个网络：NeuPL 让种群学习不再从零重来
zh.subtitle: UCL 与 DeepMind 提出 Neural Population Learning，用一个条件网络统一自博弈、虚拟博弈与 PSRO，并给出收敛保证

en.text: Why it gets cheaper: the role of transfer

NeuPL's most counterintuitive property is that discovering new strategies gets easier, not harder, as the population expands. A dedicated ablation isolates transfer to test this. A fresh agent is initialized either from scratch or by transferring the encoder and memory components of a NeuPL network trained to epoch 1,000, then asked to beat fixed Nash mixtures of increasing strength.

en.caption: Figure 6. Transferring from a NeuPL agent (left: only the green Encoder and Memory are carried over) into a fresh agent that must learn to exploit fixed Nash mixtures. Red is trained from random initialization; green transfers from epoch 1,000. Against an easily exploitable n=2 mixture the random-init agent catches up; against strong n=4 and n=7 mixtures it barely learns even with prolonged training, while transfer readily finds the exploit. Each experiment is repeated five times.

en.text: Against an easily exploitable two-policy mixture, even the from-scratch agent eventually finds a counter, just more slowly. But against competent mixtures over four or seven policies, the randomly initialized agent barely learns at all despite prolonged training, while the agent that transferred the encoder and memory readily discovers the exploit. This is the paper's central claim made concrete: the larger the population, the thicker the shared skill base, and the easier it becomes to find the next new strategy.

zh.text: 放大到时空、部分可观测的博弈
running-with-scissors 把石头剪刀布抬进了一个时空、部分可观测的设定：玩家在格子世界里移动，采集石头、布、剪刀三种资源，而且只能通过一个 4×4 的第一人称狭窄视野观察世界，必须从中推断对手隐藏的库存。这里没有精确最优反应可解，正是 PSRO 手工截断最脆弱的地方。

zh.caption: 图4 在 running-with-scissors 中，一支 NeuPL 种群逐步发展出越来越复杂、越来越多样的策略集合。交互图每 1,000 次梯度更新（一个 epoch）刷新一次。（上）随训练推进，神经种群策略之间学到的收益估计 U；（下）作为对收益矩阵响应而生成的交互图 Σ ← FPSRO-N(U)。

zh.text: 收益矩阵 U 从一片空白逐渐长出结构，交互图 Σ 也随之扩展，说明种群确实在持续发现能互相克制的新策略——而这一切都发生在同一个网络内部，早期学到的感知与操控技能被后来的策略反复复用。

en.text: The headline result: more efficient and more robust

The most telling comparison pits a NeuPL population directly against PSRO baselines representing the same set of policies. The figure below only makes sense if you read both axes together: the solid curves are Relative Population Performance (higher means better able to exploit the opponent), and the dashed purple line is the effective population size on the right axis.

en.caption: Figure 7. Relative Population Performance between a NeuPL population and the policy populations obtained by PSRO baselines; each PSRO variant is repeated over 3 trials (shaded). The dashed purple line is the effective population size: the rise in relative performance coincides with effective size growing from 5 to 8.

en.text: Two things stand out. First, a NeuPL population capped at 8 policies exploits PSRO populations of the same 8 policies — even when each PSRO iteration was given 2× the gradient updates. Second, and more importantly, the gain in relative performance coincides with the effective population size climbing from 5 to 8. That timing suggests the improvement comes from genuinely discovering new strategies rather than overfitting to old ones. Both the continued-training and from-scratch PSRO variants prove equally exploitable, which suggests they fail to build reusable representations.

zh.caption: 图1 常见的种群学习算法都可以写成同一种「交互图」（下方有向图）或等价的元博弈混合策略矩阵 Σ（上方矩阵）。图中从策略 i 指向 j、权重为 σij 的有向边，表示策略 i 以概率 σij 去对抗 j。自博弈、策略循环、虚拟博弈、PSRO-Nash 只是同一框架下 Σ 的不同取值。

zh.subtitle: UCL 与 DeepMind 提出 Neural Population Learning，用一个条件网络统一自博弈、虚拟博弈与 PSRO，并给出收敛保证

en.caption: Figure 1. Popular population-learning algorithms written as directed interaction graphs (bottom) or, equivalently, as meta-game mixture-strategy matrices Σ (top). A directed edge from policy i to j with weight σij means policy i optimizes against j with probability σij. Self-play, a strategic cycle, fictitious play, and PSRO-Nash are all just different choices of Σ within one framework.

en.text: Takeaway and honest boundaries

The one-line takeaway: hold the whole population inside a single opponent-conditioned network, let the interaction graph decide who trains against whom, and skills transfer for free across policies. That turns population learning from a sequence of wasteful from-scratch iterations into one transfer-rich training run — cheaper, still convergent, and with the surprising bonus that novel strategies become more accessible, not less, as the neural population grows.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly. The convergence guarantee applies to grounded, lower-triangular interaction graphs with a suitable solver; raising the maximum population cap beyond 8 buys only marginal improvement in exploitability; and the MuJoCo Football result is more a qualitative demonstration of feasibility than a systematic benchmark win. Even so, the through-line — carry an entire population in one conditional model — points a clear and economical way toward pushing game-theoretic population learning into genuinely complex games.

zh.text: 核心结果：更省，也更稳
最能说明问题的对照，是把 NeuPL 种群直接拿去打代表同样策略集合的 PSRO 基线。下图的关键在于两条轴要一起看：黑色实线群是相对种群表现（Relative Population Performance，越高表示越能压制对手），紫色虚线是有效种群规模（右轴）。

zh.caption: 图7 一支 NeuPL 种群与 PSRO 基线得到的策略种群之间的相对种群表现。每个 PSRO 变体重复 3 次试验，以阴影表示。紫色虚线为有效种群规模：相对表现的上升与有效种群规模从 5 增长到 8 同步发生。

zh.text: 结论有两层。其一，一支最大规模为 8 的 NeuPL 种群，能够压制由同样 8 个策略构成的 PSRO 种群——即便这些 PSRO 基线每轮迭代拿到了 2 倍的梯度更新。其二，也是更重要的一点：相对表现的提升，与有效种群规模从 5 增长到 8 是同步发生的。这说明性能的改善来自真正发现了新策略，而不是在旧策略上过拟合。无论是持续训练还是从零重训的 PSRO 变体，都同样容易被压制，暗示它们没有建立起可复用的表征。
